blocks.text: The mean, often just called the average, is the single number you get by adding up every value in a dataset and dividing by how many values there are. It is the most commonly used measure of central tendency, meaning it tries to summarize an entire collection of numbers with one representative value. This lesson opens a four part series on measures of center and position, mean, median, mode, and percentiles, each building on ideas introduced here, so pay close attention to how the mean is defined and where it can mislead you, since the next lesson on the median contrasts directly against it.

blocks.caption: The mean as a sum divided by a count

blocks.text: 1. What the Mean Represents

The mean answers a simple question: if every value in the dataset were replaced by the same single number, what number would keep the total sum unchanged? That framing is useful because it explains why the mean can land on a value that no individual data point actually has, it is a balancing point for the whole dataset, not a selection from within it.

Think of the mean as the point where a see saw balances if every data value were a weight placed along a number line at its own position. Move one weight further out and the balance point shifts toward it, which is exactly why the mean is sensitive to extreme values, a property explored in depth later in this lesson.

This balancing behavior is also why the mean is the natural summary statistic whenever you want a single number that fairly represents contributions from an entire group, from average rainfall in a city to the average score on a test.
2. The Formula for the Arithmetic Mean

For a dataset of n values, x1 through xn, the arithmetic mean is the sum of all the values divided by n. This is the formula almost everyone learns in school, and it is the default meaning of average unless a different type of mean is explicitly named.

code.content:
mean = (x1 + x2 + ... + xn) / n

# example
data = [4, 8, 6, 5, 3]
mean = (4 + 8 + 6 + 5 + 3) / 5
print(mean)   # 5.2

blocks.text: Notice the formula treats every value identically, each contributes exactly one n-th of its own value to the final result. This equal treatment is both the mean's greatest strength, simplicity and predictability, and the root of its biggest weakness, no value gets special protection from distorting the result, no matter how unusual that value is.

The formula scales cleanly to any dataset size, whether n is five values or five million, the computation is always the same sum divided by the same count, which is part of why the mean remains the default summary statistic in most reporting.
3. Computing the Mean in Code

In practice you almost never sum and divide by hand. Libraries such as numpy and pandas expose a mean function that does exactly this computation, and it is worth knowing both the manual version and the library shortcut so you can sanity check results.

code.content:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

data = [4, 8, 6, 5, 3]
print(np.mean(data))          # 5.2

series = pd.Series(data)
print(series.mean())          # 5.2

# manual version, for comparison
print(sum(data) / len(data))  # 5.2

blocks.text: All three approaches give the identical number, since they all implement the same underlying formula. The library versions become more valuable as datasets grow large or contain missing values, since numpy and pandas both offer options to handle those cases automatically.

Pandas in particular becomes essential once missing values enter the picture, since its mean method automatically skips entries marked as missing rather than treating them as zero, which would otherwise silently drag the computed average down.
4. The Mean as a Balancing Point on a Number Line

Visualizing the mean on a number line makes its balancing behavior concrete. Plot each data value as a dot, and the mean lands at the point where the dots on either side balance each other out in total distance, not necessarily in count of points.

blocks.alt: Five data points on a number line with the mean marked as the balancing point
blocks.caption: The mean sits where the total distance to points on the left equals the total distance to points on the right

blocks.text: Notice the mean does not have to sit exactly on top of any single data point, and in this picture it lands between two clusters of dots rather than in the visually densest region, precisely because it balances total distance rather than counting how many points sit on each side.

If you nudge any single point further from the cluster, the balancing point marked on the diagram would shift to follow it, a direct visual demonstration of the outlier sensitivity examined next in this lesson.
5. Weighted Mean

The plain arithmetic mean treats every value equally, but many real situations require some values to count for more than others. The weighted mean multiplies each value by its own weight before summing, then divides by the sum of the weights rather than by a plain count.

code.content:
weighted_mean = (w1*x1 + w2*x2 + ... + wn*xn) / (w1 + w2 + ... + wn)

# example: course grade from three exams with different weights
scores  = [70, 85, 95]
weights = [0.2, 0.3, 0.5]
weighted_mean = sum(w*s for w, s in zip(weights, scores)) / sum(weights)
print(weighted_mean)   # 87.5

blocks.text: A genuinely different situation from an ordinary average: a plain mean of the three scores would give 83.33, but the final exam counts for half the grade, so the weighted mean of 87.5 correctly reflects that the student did especially well on the exam that mattered most.

blocks.title: Weighted mean in survey data
blocks.content: Suppose a customer satisfaction survey oversamples a small region, so responses from that region are down weighted to 0.5 while every other response keeps a weight of 1.0, before computing the overall satisfaction mean. Without this weighting adjustment, the oversampled region would silently dominate the reported average and misrepresent the wider customer base.

blocks.text: Weighted means also appear whenever combining averages that were computed from groups of different sizes, simply averaging the group averages together without weighting by group size produces a biased combined figure.
6. Sensitivity to Outliers

Because every value contributes directly to the sum in the mean's formula, a single very large or very small value can pull the mean far away from where most of the data actually sits. This is the mean's defining weakness, and it is the exact property the median, covered in the next lesson, was designed to avoid.

code.content:
import numpy as np

salaries = [42000, 45000, 47000, 46000, 44000]
print(np.mean(salaries))   # 44800.0

# add one executive salary as an outlier
salaries_with_outlier = salaries + [900000]
print(np.mean(salaries_with_outlier))   # 187333.33

blocks.text: Adding a single outlier salary more than quadrupled the mean, from 44800 to over 187000, even though five of the six people still earn roughly 45000. Anyone reading only the mean would badly overestimate what a typical employee earns at this company.

The same distortion appears in far smaller datasets too, even a single mistyped data entry, such as an extra zero accidentally added during data entry, can shift a reported mean enough to change a business decision built on top of it.
7. Properties of the Arithmetic Mean

items: The mean of a dataset always lies between its minimum and maximum values, it can never fall outside that range.
The sum of every deviation from the mean, positive and negative combined, always equals zero, which is exactly the balancing point property described earlier.
The mean of a constant added to every value is the original mean plus that constant, and the mean of every value scaled by a constant is the original mean scaled by that same constant.
The mean is defined only for numeric data, it has no meaning for purely categorical labels such as colors or product categories.
Unlike the median or mode, the mean uses every single data value in its calculation, which is why it is efficient with information but fragile against extreme values.

blocks.text: These properties are useful for sanity checking any computed mean. If a reported mean falls outside the range of the data, or does not shift the way the scaling rule predicts, something in the calculation has gone wrong.

A quick practical check worth memorizing: if you ever compute a mean that falls outside the minimum and maximum of your dataset, you have made an arithmetic or coding error, since that outcome is mathematically impossible for a correctly computed mean.
8. Mean, Median, and Mode at a Glance

The mean is only one of several ways to describe the center of a dataset. The next three lessons in this series cover the other major options, and it helps to preview how they compare before diving into each one individually.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Measure","Definition","Sensitive to outliers","Works on non-numeric data"],"rows":[["Mean","Sum of values divided by count","Yes, strongly","No"],["Median","Middle value when sorted","No, resistant","No, needs ordering"],["Mode","Most frequently occurring value","No, resistant","Yes"]]}

blocks.text: No single measure is universally correct, the right choice depends on the shape of your data and whether outliers or non-numeric categories are present, both themes this series returns to repeatedly.

A useful habit when exploring any new dataset is to compute all three measures side by side, a large gap between the mean and median is often the fastest signal that outliers or a skewed distribution are present.
9. The Mean and Mean Squared Error Loss

The mean has a deep connection to how machine learning models are trained. If you want to pick a single number that minimizes the average squared distance to a set of data points, that number is always the mean of those points, a fact that follows directly from basic calculus.

This is why mean squared error, or MSE, is such a common loss function for regression models: minimizing it pulls a model's predictions toward the mean of the target values it is trained on, at least for a model with no other constraints. Understanding this connection makes MSE feel far less abstract, it is directly built from the same averaging operation covered throughout this lesson.

This is also why outliers in training data are so dangerous for models trained with squared error loss, the model is mathematically pulled toward accommodating those extreme points at the expense of accuracy on typical examples.
10. Mean Pooling in Embeddings

Modern language models represent each token in a piece of text as its own vector, called a token embedding. When an entire sentence or document needs to be represented as a single vector, one of the simplest and most common techniques is mean pooling, averaging all of the token embeddings together, position by position, into one combined vector.

code.content:
import numpy as np

# token_embeddings has shape (num_tokens, embedding_dim)
token_embeddings = np.random.rand(6, 4)   # 6 tokens, 4 dimensional embeddings

sentence_embedding = np.mean(token_embeddings, axis=0)
print(sentence_embedding.shape)   # (4,), one vector for the whole sentence

blocks.text: Mean pooling treats every token as equally important, exactly like the plain arithmetic mean treats every data point as equally important. More advanced pooling strategies use weighted means, giving more important tokens, such as those attended to heavily by the model, larger weights, mirroring the weighted mean concept covered earlier in this lesson.

Mean pooling remains popular precisely because it is cheap to compute and requires no additional trained parameters, unlike attention based pooling, which learns its own weighting scheme instead of treating every token equally.
11. Trimmed and Robust Variants of the Mean

Because the plain mean is so easily distorted by outliers, statisticians developed variants that keep most of the mean's simplicity while reducing its outlier sensitivity. These variants are worth knowing even though the plain mean remains the default choice in most everyday reporting.
11.1 The Trimmed Mean

A trimmed mean removes a fixed percentage of the smallest and largest values before averaging what remains. For example, a 10 percent trimmed mean drops the bottom 10 percent and top 10 percent of sorted values, then computes an ordinary mean of the middle 80 percent.

code.content:
from scipy import stats
import numpy as np

data = [42000, 45000, 47000, 46000, 44000, 900000]
print(np.mean(data))                     # 187333.33, distorted by the outlier
print(stats.trim_mean(data, 0.2))        # much closer to the typical salary

blocks.text: Trimming is a middle ground between the plain mean, which uses every value, and the median, which uses only the value or values at the very center. It is common in situations like judged competitions, where the highest and lowest scores are dropped before averaging the rest.

Choosing how much to trim is itself a tradeoff, trimming too little leaves outlier sensitivity mostly intact, while trimming too much starts to throw away legitimate data and pushes the result closer to the median than to a true mean.
12. Sample Mean Versus Population Mean

Statisticians distinguish between the mean of an entire population, every possible data point that could exist, and the mean of a sample, a smaller subset actually collected and measured. The population mean is usually written with the Greek letter mu, while the sample mean is written as x-bar.

In practice you almost always work with a sample mean, since collecting every single member of a population is rarely feasible, whether the population is every user of an app or every product ever manufactured on a production line. The sample mean is treated as an estimate of the unknown population mean, and how good that estimate is depends on how the sample was collected and how large it is.

code.content:
# notation used throughout statistics
# population mean: mu
# sample mean:     x_bar

import numpy as np
sample = [4, 8, 6, 5, 3]        # a sample drawn from some larger population
x_bar = np.mean(sample)
print(x_bar)   # an estimate of the true population mean, mu

blocks.text: This distinction matters directly in machine learning too, the average loss computed over a training batch is a sample mean, used as a practical stand in for the true, unobservable expected loss over the entire population of possible inputs.
13. Worked Example

A small online store records the number of items in each of eight recent orders: 2, 3, 2, 5, 1, 4, 2, 45. The final order was a bulk wholesale purchase, unusual compared to the typical retail customer. Compute the mean and consider what it tells you about a typical order.

code.content:
import numpy as np

orders = [2, 3, 2, 5, 1, 4, 2, 45]
print(np.mean(orders))   # 8.0

# without the wholesale order
typical_orders = [2, 3, 2, 5, 1, 4, 2]
print(np.mean(typical_orders))   # 2.71

blocks.text: The mean of all eight orders is 8.0 items, yet seven of the eight orders contain five items or fewer. Removing the single wholesale order drops the mean to about 2.71, a far more representative picture of what a typical customer actually buys. Reporting the unfiltered mean of 8.0 to a marketing team could easily lead them to badly misjudge typical basket size.

This same pattern, one unusual transaction dwarfing a batch of ordinary ones, shows up constantly in real business data, from a single large refund distorting average order value to a single downtime incident distorting average response time.
14. Common Mistakes

items: Reporting the mean of a dataset that contains extreme outliers without checking whether the median tells a meaningfully different, and often more representative, story.
Computing a plain mean when a weighted mean is actually appropriate, such as averaging per group rates without accounting for how many observations are in each group.
Trying to compute a mean on categorical data, such as averaging product category codes, which produces a number with no real meaning.
Confusing the sample mean with the true population mean, and treating a small sample's mean as if it were an exact, error free measurement.
Assuming the mean always sits near the densest cluster of data, when in fact it can land in a sparse region if outliers pull it away, as shown in the number line visualization earlier in this lesson.

blocks.title: A concrete instance of averaging without weighting
blocks.content: Suppose store A sells 10 units at an average price of 100 and store B sells 1000 units at an average price of 80. Averaging the two prices directly gives 90, but the true combined average price, weighted by units sold, is much closer to 80, since store B contributed far more units to the total.

blocks.text: 15. Practice: Compute the Mean in Code

Try this exercise yourself. Given the dataset below representing daily website visitors over two weeks, compute the plain mean, then compute the mean again after removing the single highest value, and compare the two results.

code.content:
import numpy as np

visitors = [120, 135, 128, 142, 130, 138, 125, 133, 129, 140, 131, 3500, 127, 136]

plain_mean = np.mean(visitors)
print(plain_mean)

without_outlier = [v for v in visitors if v != max(visitors)]
print(np.mean(without_outlier))

# question: which of these two numbers better describes a normal day of traffic?

blocks.text: Once you have both numbers, think about what likely happened on the day with 3500 visitors, perhaps a viral post or a marketing campaign, and why a single unusual day can so heavily bias a reported average when the mean is computed without any adjustment.

As a follow up, try replacing the single 3500 value with two smaller anomalies of 400 each and observe how the mean responds differently depending on whether the outlier mass is concentrated in one point or spread across two.
Key Takeaway

The mean summarizes a dataset by treating every value equally, summing them all and dividing by the count, which makes it simple, well understood, and mathematically convenient, it is the value that minimizes total squared distance to every point in the data. That same equal treatment of every value is also its biggest liability, a single extreme outlier can drag the mean far away from where most of the data actually lives, as the salary and order examples in this lesson demonstrated directly.

The mean shows up constantly in AI systems, from the mean squared error loss that trains regression models to the mean pooling operation that compresses many token embeddings into one vector representation. The next lesson introduces the median, a measure of center built specifically to resist the outlier sensitivity that defines the mean, using the very same salary example to make the contrast concrete.
